lesson.title: Whatever Follows: Understanding the Dependent Variable
lesson.summary: The dependent variable is the output of a function, the quantity whose value is determined entirely by the independent variable through the function's rule.
lesson.body:
The dependent variable is the variable whose value is determined by another variable, rather than chosen freely on its own. In a function, the dependent variable is just another name for the output, viewed through the lens of cause and effect: while the independent variable is the cause, freely chosen, the dependent variable is the effect, calculated from it. Its value literally depends on the independent variable's value and on the function's rule connecting the two; change the independent variable, and the dependent variable changes along with it, following whatever rule the function specifies.

In an equation like y = 3x + 4, y is the dependent variable, since its value is produced only after a value for x has been chosen and substituted in. In function notation, the entire expression f(x) represents the dependent variable; it is the output that results once the independent variable, x, has been fixed. This is consistent with everything covered earlier in this unit: the dependent variable is exactly the output, occupying the second position in an ordered pair like (x, y) or (input, output), and belonging to the range of the function rather than the domain.

Return to the rideshare example: C(m) = 1.5m + 2, where m, the miles traveled, is the independent variable, and C, the cost, is the dependent variable. The cost cannot be chosen on its own; it is entirely determined by how many miles are traveled, combined with the fixed rule of 1.5 dollars per mile plus a flat 2 dollar fee. If a rider travels 10 miles, substitute m = 10 into the rule: C(10) = 1.5(10) + 2 = 15 + 2 = 17, so the cost, the dependent variable, comes out to 17 dollars. Notice the direction of the reasoning: the rider chose 10 miles first, independently, and only afterward did the cost of 17 dollars follow as a consequence.

On a graph, the dependent variable is conventionally plotted along the vertical axis, the y-axis, matching the earlier convention that the independent variable occupies the horizontal axis. This is why range, the set of possible output values, corresponds to the bottom-to-top extent of a graph, the mirror image of domain's left-to-right extent along the independent variable's axis. Recognizing this pairing, horizontal axis with independent variable and domain, vertical axis with dependent variable and range, turns any function graph into a readable story about cause and effect rather than an abstract picture.

Learning to sort a word problem into independent and dependent variables is one of the most practical skills to come out of this whole functions unit, because it is the very first decision required before you can write a function, choose axis labels for a graph, or even decide what a table of values should record in each column. Whenever two quantities are related, ask which one is being freely chosen or controlled, and which one is only changing because the first one changed; the first answer names your independent variable, and the second names your dependent variable, closing the loop on everything this unit has built, from relation, to function, to domain and range, to input and output, to function notation and evaluation.
